front_blocks.md: Define **retention time**.

back_blocks.md: A **retention time** is the time taken for a component to travel from the injection point through the GLC column to the detector, used to identify unknown compounds by comparison with data book values.

cards.back_md: A **retention time** is the time taken for a component to travel from the injection point through the GLC column to the detector, used to identify unknown compounds by comparison with data book values.

front_blocks.md: What is used as the stationary phase in gas-liquid chromatography?

back_blocks.md: The stationary phase is a **non-polar, long-chain, non-volatile hydrocarbon** with a high boiling point, mounted onto a solid support (e.g. small silica particles packed in a glass column).

cards.front_md: What is used as the stationary phase in gas-liquid chromatography?
cards.back_md: The stationary phase is a **non-polar, long-chain, non-volatile hydrocarbon** with a high boiling point, mounted onto a solid support (e.g. small silica particles packed in a glass column).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In GLC, the mobile phase is a liquid solvent that carries sample molecules through the column.

back_blocks.md: **False.** In **GLC**, the mobile phase is an **inert carrier gas** (e.g. helium or nitrogen), not a liquid solvent.

front_blocks.md: GLC is used to analyse **..........**,  volatile liquids and solids in their **..........**  form.

back_blocks.md: GLC is used to analyse **gases**, volatile liquids and solids in their **vapour** form.

front_blocks.md: How are the retention times from a GLC chromatogram used to identify unknown compounds?

back_blocks.md: The **retention times** of sample peaks are compared with **data book values** for known compounds under the same conditions. A match identifies the unknown component.

cards.front_md: How are the retention times from a GLC chromatogram used to identify unknown compounds?
cards.back_md: The **retention times** of sample peaks are compared with **data book values** for known compounds under the same conditions. A match identifies the unknown component.

front_blocks.md: Define **gas-liquid chromatography**.

back_blocks.md: **Gas-liquid chromatography** is an analytical technique that separates volatile components of a mixture by their different interactions with a non-polar liquid stationary phase, using an inert carrier gas as the mobile phase.

cards.back_md: **Gas-liquid chromatography** is an analytical technique that separates volatile components of a mixture by their different interactions with a non-polar liquid stationary phase, using an inert carrier gas as the mobile phase.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Each peak on a GLC chromatogram represents a different volatile compound in the analysed sample.

back_blocks.md: **True.** Each **peak** on a GLC chromatogram corresponds to a different **volatile component** of the sample, with its position (retention time) used for identification.

front_blocks.md: Why do silica particles in a GLC column improve the separation of components?

back_blocks.md: Small **silica particles** provide a large **surface area**, which increases the contact between sample gas molecules and the stationary phase, improving the separation of components with similar properties.

cards.front_md: Why do silica particles in a GLC column improve the separation of components?
cards.back_md: Small **silica particles** provide a large **surface area**, which increases the contact between sample gas molecules and the stationary phase, improving the separation of components with similar properties.

front_blocks.md: In GLC, the carrier gas must be **..........**  so that it does not react with the sample molecules as they travel through the **.**.........

back_blocks.md: In GLC, the carrier gas must be **inert** so that it does not react with the sample molecules as they travel through the **column**.

front_blocks.md: Define **peak integration value**.

back_blocks.md: A **peak integration value** is the area under a peak on a GLC chromatogram, representing the relative concentration of that component in the sample mixture.

cards.back_md: A **peak integration value** is the area under a peak on a GLC chromatogram, representing the relative concentration of that component in the sample mixture.

front_blocks.md: How is the approximate percentage composition of one component calculated from a GLC chromatogram?

back_blocks.md: The **percentage** of a component = (peak area or height of that component / sum of all peak areas or heights) × 100. This gives its approximate proportion in the mixture.

front_blocks.md: The area under a GLC peak is approximated as **..........**  × base × height, treating each peak as a **.**.........

back_blocks.md: The area under a GLC peak is approximated as **½** × base × height, treating each peak as a **triangle**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Non-polar components in a GLC mixture have shorter retention times because they interact more strongly with the non-polar stationary phase.

back_blocks.md: **False.** Non-polar components have **longer** retention times because they are more attracted to the **non-polar stationary phase** and travel more slowly through the column.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

cards.back_md: **False.** Non-polar components have **longer** retention times because they are more attracted to the **non-polar stationary phase** and travel more slowly through the column.

front_blocks.md: Why do polar components tend to have shorter retention times in GLC?

back_blocks.md: **Polar components** have weaker interactions with the **non-polar stationary phase** than non-polar components do. They spend less time in the stationary phase and more time in the **mobile phase** (carrier gas), travelling faster through the column and giving shorter **retention times**.

cards.front_md: Why do polar components tend to have shorter retention times in GLC?

They spend less time in the stationary phase and more time in the **mobile phase** (carrier gas), travelling faster through the column and giving shorter **retention times**.

front_blocks.md: Define **chromatogram**.

back_blocks.md: A **chromatogram** is the output from a chromatography experiment showing peaks at different retention times, where each peak represents a separate component of the analysed mixture.

cards.back_md: A **chromatogram** is the output from a chromatography experiment showing peaks at different retention times, where each peak represents a separate component of the analysed mixture.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
If a peak in a GLC chromatogram is too small to measure its area accurately, the peak height can be used instead.

back_blocks.md: **True.** When peak areas are too small or difficult to determine, the **peak height** is used as an alternative measure of relative concentration.

front_blocks.md: Explain why compounds with lower boiling points tend to have shorter retention times in GLC.

back_blocks.md: Compounds with lower **boiling points** are more easily vaporised and spend more time in the **gaseous mobile phase**, interacting less with the stationary phase and so eluting faster.

cards.front_md: Explain why compounds with lower boiling points tend to have shorter retention times in GLC.
cards.back_md: Compounds with lower **boiling points** are more easily vaporised and spend more time in the **gaseous mobile phase**, interacting less with the stationary phase and so eluting faster.

front_blocks.md: In GLC, molecules with longer retention times are more attracted to the **..........**  stationary phase, while molecules with shorter retention times prefer to interact with the **..........**  carrier gas.

back_blocks.md: In GLC, molecules with longer retention times are more attracted to the **non-polar** stationary phase, while molecules with shorter retention times prefer to interact with the **inert** carrier gas.
